For next time: there's two places to configure the talk. The config argument to main is responsible for document-level settings (things that reveal.js doesn't allow slide-level overrides for), while metadata blocks are responsible for slide-level settings. Until a few minutes ago, the top-level metadata block could override some of the configuration settings. This was confusing.

Since this PR that I just merged, the two sets of settings are completely distinct. There's also much better custom theme support (custom themes can be packaged as Lean libraries if you want), and the docs are improved.

So, let's say it worked like this: Verso code blocks in the slides get a live parameter, like this:

```lean (live := ex1)
def x := 5
```

The show flag can be used to hide them, to do "secret setup":

```lean (live := ex1) -show
def y := 23
```
```lean (live := ex1)
#eval x + y
```

If the live parameter is present, the code block appears as normal in the slides, but also contains a little link to a live.lean-lang.org session with all preceding blocks that have the same live := on them.

At HTML build time, each live session is extracted to a file and checked by Lean, to make sure they're self-contained.

Would this do what you need?

David, I ended up using Verso Slides during the ICERM formalization of analysis workshop. Overall, I was really impressed with everything, and I much preferred using this to anything else (e.g., Beamer). The final slideshow left me with two small papercuts though.

  1. When presenting proofs, the clickable spots in a proof state only occur on each tactic. Therefore, if you have rw [foo, bar, baz], you cannot see the intermediate proof states, or else you are forced to change the source into multiple tactic calls. Similarly, you cannot click before/after a proof state. Thus, doing something like constructor; · grind; · sorry, I can't see the proof state before grind is called, because clicking on grind just says "no goals :tada: "
  2. Unlike the manual genre, in which you have the option to write {docstring List}, there was no nice and compact way for me to refer to a given declaration on its own. I didn't want to display everything for that declaration, as I wanted to refer to them inline, but I wanted users to be able to click on it for more information. However, if there were implicit arguments, this would generate errors. I therefore ended up using @ before declarations with implicit arguments. Maybe this was just user error though.

Thanks for the feedback!

I'll look at tweaking the proof state placement. Sometimes clicking twice is needed (it cycles between "show the proof state here" and "show the hover info for this identifier"), but there are some reductions from SubVerso's side to decrease the number of "bubbles" in text, and that concern isn't so relevant here. As far as before/after, the bullet before grind's post-state should be the pre-state for grind. What sort of before/after interface would work better for you?

If you want to refer to something in a slide without elaborating it as a term, you can write {name}`List` in the text. Clicking it should open a box with info. Does that work for what you need?
Ah, the {name}`List` feature is the thing I was missing!

I realized that the grind complaint I was making above wasn't actually about my ICERM slides, but about a different trial presentation using verso slides I gave to my department. I don't have a public-facing url to point you to there, but the example is easy enough to copy. It's the default example at lean-lang.org:

/-- A prime is a number larger than 1 with no trivial divisors -/
def IsPrime (n : Nat) := 1 < n ∧ ∀ k, 1 < k → k < n → ¬ k ∣ n

/-- Every number larger than 1 has a prime factor -/
theorem exists_prime_factor :
    ∀ n, 1 < n → ∃ k, IsPrime k ∧ k ∣ n := by
  intro n h1
  -- Either `n` is prime...
  by_cases hprime : IsPrime n
  · grind [Nat.dvd_refl]
  -- ... or it has a non-trivial divisor with a prime factor
  · obtain ⟨k, _⟩ : ∃ k, 1 < k ∧ k < n ∧ k ∣ n := by
      simp_all [IsPrime]
    obtain ⟨p, _, _⟩ := exists_prime_factor k (by grind)
    grind [Nat.dvd_trans]

If you put this into a verso slide (I just copied it into the demo version to test it again), you'll note that there is no where you can click to see what happens between the start of the second bullet and the end goal state. Clicking obtain just gives you information about the tactic, but you can't cycle through to see the goal state afterwards.
So maybe the actual problem is that it's not displaying the post-state for obtain.
That's certainly possible. Getting the nested rw steps rendering has totally blown my slide time budget for the next little bit, so I created an issue - thanks!
Thanks for working on it!
This PR makes the nested highlighting of sub-proof-states in rw work correctly. Thanks for the push on this.

Is it possible to have one Lean project with multiple slideshows, without having to make one executable per slideshow?

I guess this works as a workaround for now

import VersoTest.Slideshow1
import VersoTest.Slideshow2
import VersoSlides

open VersoSlides

def main : IO UInt32 := do
  let returnCode1 ← slidesMain
    (config := { theme := "black", slideNumber := true, transition := "slide" })
    (doc := %doc VersoTest.Slideshow1)
  if returnCode1 ≠ 0 then return returnCode1
  IO.FS.rename "_slides/index.html" "_slides/1.html"

  let returnCode2 ← slidesMain
    (config := { theme := "black", slideNumber := true, transition := "slide" })
    (doc := %doc VersoTest.Slideshow2)
  if returnCode2 ≠ 0 then return returnCode2
  IO.FS.rename "_slides/index.html" "_slides/2.html"

  return 0

*
  * Type
  * Description
  * Example elements

  * {lean}`Nat`
  *  The natural numbers/nonnegative integers. Can be arbitrarily large.
  * `0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...`

  * `..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`

This seemed to work (recalling that a :::: directive needs more colons than any ::: directive it encloses):

:::::attr (style := "font-size: 0.8em")

*
  * Type
  * Description
  * Example elements
*
  * {lean}`Nat`
  * :::attr (style := "font-size: 0.6em")
    The natural numbers/nonnegative integers. Can be arbitrarily large.
    :::
  * `0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ...`
*
  * {lean}`Int`
  * The integers
  * `..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...`
*
  * {lean}`String`
  * Unicode text
  * `"apple"`, `"banana"`
::::
:::::

However, even if I set the inner :::attr to be the same size as the outer :::::attr, the inner text was still much smaller. Nevermind, this is because em is a relative size.

I still wonder if there's an easier or more idiomatic way to do this. Also, is there a way to change the relative lengths of the columns, so as to make the middle column larger?

You could try rem instead of em, perhaps?

There's no current way to adjust the column widths by hand here. This would be a reasonable thing to have, though. I'll think about an appropriate way to specify that.
As far as the executables goes, you found a good solution. What's the specific use case? That can inform further thoughts about good ways to improve the process of generating output from Verso.

I am trying to prepare some lecture slides for several lectures and would like to keep them in the same repository, but have each lecture be its own slideshow. Ideally I would like it so that all the .html files can be in the same directory (which is not solved by multiple executables, since if I had that the different index.html files would overwrite each other).

This makes a lot of sense, thanks. Having the executables configured to output to different locations seems like one potential solution here.

For my understanding: why is sharing a directory important? Would it be enough to put each rendered show in its own directory? That is, instead of slides/show1.html and slides/show2.html, have slides/show1/index.html and slides/show2/index.html? This avoids issues with things like images clobbering each other as well.

It would also be not a ton of code to implement your own slidesMain that does multiple shows at once, outputting them as is useful for you. This could ensure that assets don't clobber each other.

Yeah that could work. My thought was that I could avoid duplicating the reveal.js by having all the .html files in the same directory but the actual javascript and CSS size is only 3.2 MB so it probably doesn't matter. Hypothetically, all the lectures could reference the same large image, and then you want those images to clobber each other to save space, but this isn't necessary for me and it probably doesn't matter.

It would be nice to be able to generate all the slides with a single command rather than one executable per slideshow, but this can already be done without any change needed on the verso side.

One issue I am running into when doing multi-slideshow presentations is that the constants defined in code blocks in different slideshows can conflict with each other. I might have two presentations which both contain a slide like

# My favorite slide

We can define a jabberwocky as a collection of foos. This lets us state the following:
```lean
theorem my_theorem : True := trivial
```

The problem is that if I have two slideshows which both define some constant my_theorem inside code blocks, then when both of them are imported into the same file it causes a conflict since my_theorem is in the global namespace. This can be resolved either by using leanModule (I think) or by adding a namespace like Hidden (as long as each file uses a different Hidden namespace). The namespace can be pedagogically bad sometimes since then #check prints it out, but it's probably fine most of the time. But this does show that you can't always combine multiple independent verso documents to all get rendered in the same executable.

That's a good point.

We're already working on a way to run Verso without importing the document into an executable - this will also be good for compile times, because it won't go try to generate C code for Mathlib :-)

In the meantime, my suggestion for you is perhaps a bit boring, but it should work predictably: have a boilerplate exe for each lecture, and a script or a Makefile or custom Lake target that runs them when needed. This is not the most elegant solution, but I suspect it'll be reliable and not take much actual work to get set up.
I think that's good enough for me in the meantime.
Next time I have some time to work on the slide package, I'll keep this multi-slideshow use case in mind. I suspect you're not the only one doing a lecture series.
